atoms.text: The p-zombie: a being physically identical to a person but with no inner experience behaves exactly like one, so the story can populate a world with perfect impostors.
The pain that is not felt: a body reacts to injury without suffering, so the observer cannot distinguish agony from performance.
The behavioral test: every experiment measures response, not experience, so science can never confirm whether anyone is home.
The identical twin who is empty: a duplicate is created with all memories and mannerisms but no consciousness, so intimacy is haunted by the possibility of a hollow copy.
The conceivability argument: if a zombie world can be imagined without contradiction, physicalism may be false, so the story's plot turns on what can be conceived.
The philosopher who suspects everyone: a researcher treats all colleagues as possible zombies, so ordinary trust collapses into an unfalsifiable doubt.
The zombie who passes every test: an entity without experience is indistinguishable from a person in every measurable way, so institutions cannot exclude it.
The hard problem: subjective experience resists physical explanation, so the story's central mystery is not a crime but the fact of feeling.
The imitation man: an artificial person is built to mimic emotion so well that no one can tell, so the uncanny is normalized by good engineering.
The one who claims to be a zombie: a person insists they feel nothing, so testimony becomes the only evidence and it may be a lie.
The coffee that tastes like nothing: a subtle difference in experience separates two physically identical people, so the smallest sensory detail becomes proof of a soul.
The factory of identical bodies: mass production creates thousands of physically identical beings, so the story can ask which one, if any, is conscious.
The philosopher who says we are all zombies: a thinker argues that consciousness is an illusion, so the characters must defend their own interiority.
The zombie's rights: a being without experience demands legal protection, so personhood is detached from sentience.
The test that cannot be run: a procedure would reveal whether a subject is conscious, but it requires destroying the subject, so certainty is lethal.
The narrator who might be hollow: the story is told from inside a mind that cannot prove it has one, so the reader's trust is the final experiment.
